typeName: Q3: Inference (a test or an interval)
title: Summer jobs: a two-proportion interval and the claims it supports

stimulus.title: Summer jobs for juniors and seniors
stimulus.html:
A large school district wants to compare its juniors and seniors. It selects a random sample of 220 seniors and, separately, a random sample of 250 juniors, and asks each student whether they already have a summer job lined up. (Invented data.)
Students with a summer job lined up
GroupHave a job lined upSample size
Seniors121220
Juniors105250

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify an appropriate inference procedure for estimating the difference between the proportion of all seniors and the proportion of all juniors in the district who have a summer job lined up, define the parameter, and verify the conditions for the procedure.

rubric.point: Names a two-sample z interval for a difference in proportions and defines the parameter p_S - p_J in context (true proportions of all seniors and all juniors in the district with a summer job lined up).
accept: two-proportion z interval for p_S - p_J
a 2-proportion z interval with p_J - p_S defined clearly in context

rubric.point: Checks random and 10%: two independent random samples, and 220 is less than 10% of the district's seniors and 250 is less than 10% of its juniors.
accept: states both samples are random and independent, and that each sample is under 10% of its population

rubric.point: Checks large counts with numbers: 121, 99, 105 and 145 are each at least 10.
accept: n_S p-hat_S = 121, n_S(1 - p-hat_S) = 99, n_J p-hat_J = 105, n_J(1 - p-hat_J) = 145, all at least 10 (5 is also accepted as the threshold)

parts.sample:
Two-sample z interval for p_S - p_J, where p_S is the true proportion of all seniors in the district with a summer job lined up and p_J is the true proportion of all juniors in the district with one.
Random: the problem says two separate random samples, one of seniors and one of juniors, so the samples are independent.
10%: 220 is less than 10% of all seniors in a large district, and 250 is less than 10% of all juniors.
Large counts: 121, 220 - 121 = 99, 105 and 250 - 105 = 145 are each at least 10.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference. Show the expression with the values substituted.

rubric.point: Shows the correct expression with values: (0.55 - 0.42) +/- 1.96*sqrt(0.55*0.45/220 + 0.42*0.58/250).
accept: the same expression for p-hat_J - p-hat_S
the general formula with the four values substituted

rubric.point: Gives the correct interval, from about 0.040 to 0.220 (or from -0.220 to -0.040 for juniors minus seniors).
accept: an interval from technology matching to two decimal places
the margin of error 0.090 with the center 0.13

parts.label: c

rubric.point: Uses confidence language about capturing the parameter: "We are 95% confident that the interval ... captures ...".
accept: "we are 95% confident the true difference is between ... and ..."

rubric.point: Names the parameter in context with the order of subtraction: the true difference in the proportions of all seniors and all juniors in the district with a summer job lined up (seniors minus juniors).
accept: the true difference p_S - p_J described in context

parts.sample: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.040 to 0.220 captures the true difference in the proportions of all seniors and all juniors in the district who have a summer job lined up (seniors minus juniors).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A counselor makes two claims: (i) seniors in the district are more likely than juniors to have a summer job lined up; (ii) the proportion of seniors with a job lined up is 25 percentage points higher than the proportion of juniors. Justify whether the interval supports each claim.

rubric.point: Claim (i): because every value in the interval is greater than 0, the interval gives convincing evidence that the true proportion of seniors with a job lined up is greater than that of juniors.
accept: 0 is not in the interval and the plausible differences are positive, so claim (i) is supported; the reason uses the interval, not only the sample difference of 0.13

rubric.point: Claim (ii): because 0.25 is greater than every value in the interval, 0.25 is not a plausible difference, so the interval gives convincing evidence against claim (ii) (the true difference is less than 25 points).
accept: 0.25 is outside the interval, so claim (ii) is not supported; the reason uses the interval, not only the sample difference

parts.sample:
(i) Because every value in the interval from 0.040 to 0.220 is greater than 0, the interval gives convincing evidence that the true proportion of all seniors in the district with a summer job lined up is greater than the true proportion of all juniors with one. The interval supports claim (i).
(ii) A difference of 25 percentage points is 0.25. Because 0.25 is greater than every value in the interval, it is not a plausible value for p_S - p_J. The interval gives convincing evidence that the true difference is less than 0.25, so it does not support claim (ii).

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain what the phrase "95% confidence" means in this context.

rubric.point: Describes the capture rate of the method in repeated sampling: about 95% of intervals from many pairs of random samples of these sizes would capture the true difference p_S - p_J.
accept: "if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true difference in proportions"

parts.sample: If the district took many pairs of random samples of 220 seniors and 250 juniors and built a 95% interval from each pair, about 95% of those intervals would capture the true difference between the proportions of all seniors and all juniors with a summer job lined up.
